**Ad ranking needs meaningful probabilities, not just a useful order.** In many auctions, predicted click or conversion probabilities interact with bids and value estimates. Two models can rank examples similarly yet assign very different probability scales, producing different allocation, pricing, or advertiser-value outcomes under the auction's rules.

**A calibration example.** If ads predicted at 10% click probability actually receive clicks only 2% of the time, the model is overconfident in that slice. High AUC does not fix this: AUC measures ordering, not whether 0.10 means ten clicks per hundred comparable impressions. Evaluate calibration separately from ranking quality. [3](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

**Delayed conversions create unfinished labels.** A user may convert several days after a click. Treating yesterday's unconverted clicks as permanent negatives systematically undercounts eventual conversions. Use mature-label windows, delay-aware estimation, or an appropriate survival model, and backfill outcomes without duplicating events.

**Build a bounded serving path.** Precompute expensive embeddings and aggregates, fetch fresh features with timeouts, score quickly, then apply the actual auction and pacing rules. Keep a fallback when features are missing. Do not assume every ad system is a simple bid-times-pCTR generalized second-price auction; define the mechanism first.

Evaluate spend, advertiser return, user experience, fraud, and budget interactions. Marketplace interference means one advertiser's changed allocation can affect others, complicating naive experiments. A model is successful only if its probability estimates and serving behavior support the economic decision being made, not merely because an offline classification metric increased.

**Technical details and references.**

An auction needs scores comparable across ads, so biased pCTR/pCVR changes both allocation and bid/value interpretation. The exact score depends on the auction and charging model; do not assume every system uses a simple pCTR×bid GSP rule. Train on timestamped impressions/clicks and calibrate by important traffic segments, with separate validation of ranking and probability error.

For conversions delayed up to seven days, recent nonconversions are censored rather than final negatives. Use mature-label datasets, delayed-feedback models, or survival/eventual-conversion estimates, then backfill outcomes idempotently. Preserve impression/click identity through attribution and avoid leaking late conversions into earlier feature snapshots.

Serve cached embeddings and bounded real-time features with a fast model, and monitor calibration drift, auction outcomes, spend/pacing, and fraud. Randomized experiments must consider marketplace interference and advertiser budgets. Optimize business value with user-experience constraints; a model that improves AUC can still harm revenue or advertiser return if its probabilities are miscalibrated.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For a specified value-based scoring model, expected value may involve $pCTR\times pCVR\times value$, but auction rules determine how that enters allocation/payment. Small probability bias can therefore affect economic outcomes even when rank AUC is unchanged. Evaluate calibration by age of label and traffic slice, and distinguish unobserved future conversions from confirmed negatives. [3](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://ai.meta.com/blog/dlrm-an-advanced-open-source-deep-learning-recommendation-model/) and [2](https://wnzhang.net/share/rtb-papers/delayed-feedback.pdf).
